title: E.J. Carroll, ‘Law & Order,’ ‘GTA 5’ and ‘Blue Bloods’ Actor, Dies at 66
description:

	Carroll died s
body:
E.J. Carroll, who appeared in projects including “The Deuce,” “Law & Order” and “Grand Theft Auto V,” died on Thursday. He was 66.

	Carroll died suddenly Thursday morning, his rep confirmed to Variety. No cause of death has been provided.

	Throughout his nearly 30-year career, Carroll’s credits included Darren Aronfsky’s “The Wrestler” and Robert De Niro and Kate Beckinsale’s “Everybody’s Fine,” as well as “The Cake Eaters,” “The Capers,” “The Winning Season,” “The Hungry Ghosts” and “A Fish Story.” One of the actor’s most recognizable roles was as Fat Mooney in HBO’s “The Deuce,” where his character ran a sex shop owned by Frankie Martino (James Franco).
	

	Born on May 21, 1960, Carroll made his on-screen debut in 1998 as a police officer in “Law & Order,” later returning for two episodes of “Law & Order: SVU” and an additional two in “Law & Order: Criminal Intent.” As a guest star, Carroll appeared in projects such as “The Blacklist,” “Blue Bloods,” “High Maintenance,” “Pose” and “The Punisher.” He also starred as Sheriff Victor Sickles in two episodes of Terence Winter and Martin Scorsese’s “Boardwalk Empire” in 2012 before going on to appear in an episode of “Damages,” which starred Glenn Close and Rose Byrne, that same year.

	He also voiced a character in “Grand Theft Auto V” in 2013 and played Dr. Scott in the concert version of “The Rocky Horror Show,” titled “The Rocky Horror Tribute Show.” The concert ran for one night in 2007 to raise money for cancer charities Acting for a Cure and Komen for the Cure.
	

	Prior to his death, Carroll most recently starred in “A Delicate Arrangement,” the upcoming Vivian Leigh biopic. Starring Carla Gugino as the “Gone With the Wind” actress, the film is written and produced by Jayce Bartok and directed by Nick Sandow.

title: Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures Forge Partnership to Co-Produce a Slate of Films From the ‘Global South’
description: Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures have announced a strategic partnership to develop and co-produce a slate of films “championing visio
body:
Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures have announced a strategic partnership to develop and co-produce a slate of films “championing visionary filmmakers and compelling stories from the Global South and beyond with an emphasis on culturally authentic storytelling and broad international appeal,” they said in a statement.

	The Global South is a geopolitical and economic term that broadly includes countries in Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, most of Asia, and most of Oceania.
	

	The Qatar Film Committee is an official body that is part of the Media City Qatar hub and is tasked with driving growth of the country’s entertainment industry.

	Founded in April 2024 by brothers Badie Ali and Hamza Ali, Chicago-based Watermelon Pictures has gained worldwide attention in its short time in business with releases such as Rashid Masharawi’s “From Ground Zero,” Annemarie Jacir’s “Palestine 36” and Cherien Dabis’ “All That’s Left of You,” which were shortlisted for the best international feature Oscar, as well as Kaouther ben Hania’s Oscar-nominated “The Voice of Hind Rajab.”

	The partnership between Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon was announced on the second day of the Doha Film Festival’s Industry Days, which are running from Nov. 19-21.

	The plan is for the pact to spawn a slate of projects developed by Watermelon spanning comedy, television, genre and drama. Financial terms were not disclosed.

	“Combining Qatar’s commitment to world-class filmmaking, growing production capabilities, and investment in the creative economy with Watermelon’s access to leading talent, established distribution infrastructure, and deep understanding of what resonates with audiences, the collaboration aims to produce commercially compelling films with high production values and international appeal,” the statement said.
	

	The plan envisions that these projects will shoot mainly in Qatar or be structured as Qatari co-productions. They will tap into the country’s growing production ecosystem and the Qatar Screen Production Incentive rebate offering up to 50% in cash, “creating opportunities for local crews, businesses and creative talent while strengthening Qatar’s position as an international production hub,” it noted.

	“Through this partnership, we want to give filmmakers the resources to tell stories rooted in their communities and bring them to audiences around the world,” Hassan Al Thawadi, the Qatari lawyer who chairs the Qatar Film Committee, said in the statement. 

	For Watermelon Pictures, the partnership marks a significant leap into larger-scale, mainstream production, backed by its distribution expertise.

schema.headline: Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures Forge Partnership to Co-Produce a Slate of Films From the ‘Global South’

title: ‘The Tree’ Director Julie Bertuccelli Tells IFFI Masterclass a Canadian Producer Stole Her ‘Italian Shoes’ Adaptation, Readies India-Set Feature
description: French filmmaker Julie Bertuccelli, whose “The Tree” closed the Cannes Film Festival in 2010, said her planned adaptation of Henning Mankell’s nove
body:
French filmmaker Julie Bertuccelli, whose “The Tree” closed the Cannes Film Festival in 2010, said her planned adaptation of Henning Mankell’s novel “Italian Shoes” fell apart after a Canadian producer “stole the film” from her, and that she plans to shoot her next feature in India.

	Bertuccelli was speaking at “From Witness to Change: The Social Responsibility of Documentary Cinema,” a masterclass at the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, moderated by Indian filmmaker Haobam Paban Kumar.
	

	Responding to an audience question, Bertuccelli said she set out to adapt the Mankell book five years ago. She wrote the script and cast the film, which was due to shoot in Canada, before the pandemic brought everything to a halt.

	“In fact there is a bad Canadian producer who stole the film from me,” Bertuccelli said. She did not name the producer and declined to give the full account. She said she was forced to cancel the project, adding: “I worked for quite four years, five years for nothing because they stole from me, they stole, you know, the movie and I could not do it. So it was very hard.”

	Bertuccelli turned to the directors in the room. “It’s a fight against you, against yourself, because you need to work, you need even when you are depressed or you have doubts, you need to continue, because the only thing that makes you a director is that you go on and you never, you know, you never stop your desire,” she said.

	She is now writing the new feature. It follows a French woman living in Mumbai who is slowly going blind and sets off on one last journey with her son, who is half Indian and half French. Bertuccelli plans to come to India to make it.
	

	“It’s my first time in India, but for so long I’m admiring your country, your culture,” she said.

	Bertuccelli is also finishing a second documentary alongside “The Violin Lesson,” which follows Rachel Routier, a violin teacher in Pantin, outside Paris, and is headed for French cinemas after airing on France Télévisions in September. She hopes to screen “The Violin Lesson” in Mumbai in the coming weeks, along with either “The Tree” or “Since Otar Left.”

	During two terms as president of La Scam, the French authors’ society for documentary makers, Bertuccelli created the Golden Eye documentary prize at Cannes, whose Indian winners include Payal Kapadia’s “A Night of Knowing Nothing” and Shaunak Sen’s “All That Breathes.” She also founded La Cinémathèque du documentaire in Paris, which hopes to stage a retrospective of Indian documentary.

	Asked by Kumar whether documentary carries a social responsibility, Bertuccelli said: “For sure there is a big responsibility because the film can change the life of somebody, you know?”

	She pointed to “School of Babel,” which followed a class for children newly arrived in France. The film was widely seen by school groups and shifted young viewers’ attitudes toward immigrant classmates, she said, and it helped protect such classes at a time when some were being closed. “Because I said with this film to all the Education Ministry: ‘So I made a film to show that France is great, but don’t touch it. Now you can’t destroy this,'” she said.

	Kumar later asked where cinema stands in the age of AI. Bertuccelli allowed that the technology can be useful for small tasks, such as sound work.

	“But I hate AI. Not just because, okay, it’s dangerous for us, we will forget how to have memory, how to think by ourselves. Also because they steal, they stole the film, you know, they stole the author rights. But also more because it’s an ecological, horrible, horrible thing,” she said.

	Documentary, she argued, is cinema’s last line of defense, because “there is a contract with you that when you see a documentary, there is reality, there is truth.” She added that “the 21st century will be the one of documentary.”

	Bertuccelli spent around 15 years as an assistant to directors including Krzysztof Kieślowski, Bertrand Tavernier and Otar Iosseliani before making her own documentaries. Her fiction debut, “Since Otar Left,” shot in Georgia, won the Critics’ Week grand prize at Cannes and the César for best first film. Her documentary work includes “School of Babel,” “Latest News From the Cosmos” and “Jane Campion, the Cinema Woman.” “The Tree,” starring Charlotte Gainsbourg, played IFFI more than 15 years ago, but Bertuccelli could not attend as she was eight months pregnant at the time.
	

	She closed the session by pointing back to the Lumière brothers, whose operators traveled the world filming everyday life.

	“Cinema was born documentary and it will die documentary,” she said.

schema.headline: ‘The Tree’ Director Julie Bertuccelli Tells IFFI Masterclass a Canadian Producer Stole Her ‘Italian Shoes’ Adaptation, Readies India-Set Feature

title: ‘Godavari’ Director Nikhil Mahajan Turns a Malegaon Carjacking Into Neo-Noir With WAVES Film Bazaar Project ‘Mongoose’
description: Nikhil Mahajan, the Indian National Film Award-winning director of “Godavari” and the Netflix series “Betaal,” is bringing “Mongoose,” a Marathi-la
body:
Nikhil Mahajan, the Indian National Film Award-winning director of “Godavari” and the Netflix series “Betaal,” is bringing “Mongoose,” a Marathi-language neo-noir thriller about a cab driver and the con man who steals his taxi, to the Co-Production Market at WAVES Film Bazaar.

	Set in the hardscrabble town of Malegaon, the film follows Abhimanyu, a hardworking driver whose hopes of owning his own taxi are wrecked when he is carjacked on the highway. The thief, Shahrukh, is a debt-ridden hustler who crashes the stolen cab, killing pilgrims traveling in a van, and the two men’s lives become violently entangled. As Abhimanyu chases justice and Shahrukh tries to stay free, it emerges that Abhimanyu’s own boss ordered the hit.
	

	Mahajan says that, particularly since “Raavsaaheb,” he has been drawn to subjects that let him examine Indian society through a social lens, and that “Mongoose” digs into the gap between ambition and reality for one section of the population. “I choose to lend my genre sensibility to these social subjects to create a more wide appealing introspection of the Indian living condition.”

	Suhrud Godbole and Mahajan’s Coquelicot Pictures is producing with Sydney-based Photoplay Films. The budget is $1.1 million, with $650,000 in place. The project is in advanced development and the team aims to start prep in the second quarter of 2027. In Goa, they are looking for co-producers, sales agents and “early-stage festival programmers.”

	“At Coquelicot Pictures we are very driven and passionate about creating and supporting modern and cutting-edge storytelling. ‘Mongoose’ is a story we believe will cut across languages and demographics, and Nikhil is one of the finest genre-makers we have in the country today,” says Godbole, who has worked with Mahajan since 2011. “In Karen Radzyner we have the perfect partner to collaborate and take this film to the world.”
	

	Radzyner leads Photoplay’s film and TV arm. The company’s films and series have competed at Berlin, Venice, Toronto, CanneSeries and SeriesFest, and its executive producer credits include “Goldstone,” “Berlin Syndrome” and “Sweet Country.”

	“Nikhil’s storytelling blew me away at our first meeting in Goa two years ago and watching his festival-darling, award-winning films cemented that he’s a writer/director with soul, who alongside his impressive producer Suhrud (at Coquelicot Pictures), opens windows of insight into India for a global audience,” Radzyner says.

	Mahajan’s features also include “Pune 52” and “Baji.” “Godavari” premiered at the Vancouver International Film Festival and won him the Indian National Film Award for best direction as well as a special jury award for best director at IFFI. “Betaal” was produced by Blumhouse Television and Red Chillies Entertainment. Coquelicot released “Tighee” in theaters in March.

	Mahajan says he hopes audiences unfamiliar with these issues get “a ringside view of reality,” and that international viewers see “a side of India which is seldom seen.” Next up for him is a horror musical, which starts filming soon.

	WAVES Film Bazaar runs as the market component of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

title: Robert Pattinson’s 007 Movie in Talks to Shoot at Pinewood as Studio Says ‘We’re the Home of Bond’
description: Corporate affairs director of the U.K.’s famed Pinewood Studios, Andrew M. Smith, said he cannot yet confirm whether or not the next Bond film will
body:
Corporate affairs director of the U.K.’s famed Pinewood Studios, Andrew M. Smith, said he cannot yet confirm whether or not the next Bond film will be shot on their lot, but that he and his team are keeping their “fingers crossed.”

	Speaking at a panel about locations at the Doha Industry Days moderated by Variety’s Nick Vivarelli, Smith said he “wishes” he could talk about whether or not the franchise will return to Pinewood but it’s still early days. “I’m thrilled that Bond’s been announced,” he said. “We’re talking about it. We’re the home of Bond. Fingers crossed.”
	

	Bond movies shot at Pinewood go back from the very first film, 1962’s “Dr. No.” Out of 25 Bond movies, only two did not shoot at the lot: 1989’s “License to Kill” and 1995’s “GoldenEye.” The former shot primarily in Mexico and Florida, while the latter was filmed in Leavesden as Pinewood was booked for “First Knight.” “GoldenEye” did, however, complete sound mixing at Pinewood.

	Five days ago, the film world came to a brief halt when Robert Pattinson was announced as the new 007 following months of speculation on who would take on the sacred tuxedo from Daniel Craig. Craig’s five-movie run as the womanizing super spy began in 2006 with “Casino Royale” and ended with 2021’s “No Time to Die,” which ends with Bond sacrificing himself to save the world from a secret global terrorist organization.

	“No Time to Die” was also the last film in the series released before longtime producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli sold creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM for $20 million.
	

	Amazon currently has a major long-term deal with Pinewood’s sister location in the U.K., Shepperton Studios, where it has taken 9 stages of a recently opened 17-sound stage expansion. However, Bond will unlikely find much space there, with it currently housing “Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” and season 4 expected to go into production in early 2028. 

	Elsewhere in the conversation, Smith also spoke about attracting major U.S. productions to the U.K. thanks to a combination of healthy tax rebates, top infrastructure and highly-skilled crews. “You’ve got to have good infrastructure, you’ve got to have a good skill base, and you’ve got to have good incentives. But I think the incentive is probably [the bigger attraction].”

	“I mean, we heard yesterday from Steven Paul that his film about President Nixon is being filmed in the U.K. Is Pinewood better than Paramount? No. It’s the money,” he added, noting how he doesn’t believe American productions are flocking to the U.K. because of any key differences in either infrastructure or crews.

	The veteran believes, however, that they have been “very fortunate” in their positioning in the U.K., particularly when it comes to keeping 59 of their 61 stages under lease by major American studios like Disney and Netflix. Out of 38 Marvel films, for example, 21 have been shot at Pinewood.

	“Would you invest in any more stages in mature markets? I don’t think you would at the moment. I think what we’re trying to do is innovate for the future,” he said. “In new markets you need to think very carefully about building new stages. There’s a lot of empty stages in the world right now, especially in mature markets.”

	For now, Pinewood is keeping its eye on Bond, but also branching out to new technology, content creation and short-form. The studios recently struck a partnership with the U.K. government for the CoSTAR Network, a £75.6 million investment by the UKRI Infrastructure Fund and delivered by the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC). Based at Pinewood Studios, it is a national hub for creative businesses to “test and take new ideas to market […] strengthening the U.K.’s standing as a world leader in creative technology,” according to a Pinewood statement.
	

	At the panel, Smith emphasized the importance of embracing technology and new formats, noting how content creators working on moving into long-form content might be “the next Russo Brothers.”

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson’s 007 Movie in Talks to Shoot at Pinewood as Studio Says ‘We’re the Home of Bond’

title: Bill Maher Mocks ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’-Playing Young Men With Awful ICE Joke
description: The Season 24 finale of “Real Time with Bill Maher” aired Friday night — it’s been renewed for two more seasons through 2028 — and the crabby comic
body:
The Season 24 finale of “Real Time with Bill Maher” aired Friday night — it’s been renewed for two more seasons through 2028 — and the crabby comic’s monologue tackled everything from the spate of tech outages to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s infidelity to “Grand Theft Auto 6.”

	“It’s getting a little scary out there,” offered Maher. “Last week, it was Microsoft and the airlines that went down. This week: Apple — whew that’s a big one — four of the big banks, the National Security Agency. My god, for several hours, we had no idea who Jensen Huang was fucking.”
	

	He continued: “This is just AI doing its thing: finding vulnerabilities. They’re fixing shit by breaking shit. Didn’t we try this with DOGE? Wasn’t that the same thing? OK, but here’s my question: If these are not cyberattacks, why yesterday did they fire the top official in charge of cybersecurity? It’s like your wife saying, ‘You know, I’m definitely not having an affair, but I fired the pool boy yesterday.’”

	Then, the 70-year-old political pundit took aim at the cultural phenomenon that is “GTA 6,” which hit a whopping $3.79 billion in first-day sales and led to tons of people calling out of work to play it on their PlayStation 5 or Xbox.

	“Apple? Oh my gosh. I mean, I worry for young men. Really, without the phone, anyone hoping to see tits will have to talk to an actual girl,” he joked. “And if you think that joke is stereotypical or unfair, I will just remind you that ‘Grand Theft Auto’ came out yesterday, and about a fifth of the young men in America stayed home and didn’t go to work to play a game. This thing has caused more workplace absences than ICE.”

schema.headline: Bill Maher Mocks ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’-Playing Young Men With Awful ICE Joke

title: Indian Auteur Girish Kasaravalli Looks Back on 50 Years of Cinema at IFFI Masterclass: ‘All My Films Talk About Othering’
description: Indian auteur Girish Kasaravalli looked back on his career in Kannada-language cinema at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Go
body:
Indian auteur Girish Kasaravalli looked back on his career in Kannada-language cinema at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, in a masterclass titled “The Moral Universe of Parallel Cinema: 50 Years of Girish Kasaravalli.” 

	The 75-year-old spoke about the moral contradictions of society and the relationship between cinematic form and social content. He also argued that even entertainment is a political act. The session was moderated by Variety‘s Asia editor Naman Ramachandran.
	

	Across films such as “Ghatashraddha” (1977), “Tabarana Kathe” (1986), “Thaayi Saheba” (1997), “Dweepa” (2002) and “Gulabi Talkies” (2008), Kasaravalli has kept returning to one question: how societies exclude individuals and communities, and how people who are themselves victims of oppressive structures can also become complicit in perpetuating them.

	Asked whether the 1977 Kannada classic “Ghatashraddha,” which examines religious orthodoxy and social exclusion, still spoke to contemporary India, Kasaravalli said: “All my films talk about othering. I always talk about how society looks at some people from a different lens, and in that process they make them ‘other.'” He described this as “the biggest cruelty an individual or a group of people can impart on another person.”

	Asked whether he considered himself a political filmmaker, Kasaravalli said: “Whoever makes something, whether he makes mainstream cinema or art cinema, he is making a political statement, either in support of the dominant ideology or opposing the dominant ideology. He cannot avoid it.” There is nothing called only entertainment, he added, and even entertainment is a political form.
	

	On his characters, he said: “I don’t want any of my characters to become a kind of a mouthpiece to a certain ideology.” Drawing on Jean-Luc Godard, he compared understanding a character to buying a house: one must examine it from the outside and then from within before making a judgment. Similarly, a filmmaker must inhabit a character and then step back to assess it. For Kasaravalli, characters are too complex for a filmmaker to easily take sides.

	On the evolution of his cinematic language, Kasaravalli described the visual construction of “Ghatashraddha,” as “ritualistic cinema.” “The style is not imposed on it; it comes from within the content itself,” he said. Since “Ghatashraddha” was about a ritual, he felt its cinematic form should reflect that structure.

	Kasaravalli said he could not write a script until he had clarity about its images. “For me, the film is not merely making statements; it’s an attempt by the filmmaker to impart an experience.” He described writing detailed instructions for his crew, down to which hand a character uses to lift a glass, because even that changes the composition of a shot.

	This attention to the relationship between character and environment shaped “Gulabi Talkies.” Kasaravalli told cinematographer S. Ramachandra that the coastal community had to be as important as the protagonist. He wanted the images to feel like “actuality coverage,” not a predetermined visual construction. Rejecting conventional scenic shots of the sea and rocks, he told his cinematographer: “Film should not have any pretty image.” They chose 16mm, allowing the grain to contribute to the film’s sense of actuality.

	The discussion of visual aesthetics brought him to Cuban filmmaker Julio García Espinosa’s idea of “imperfect cinema,” which, for Kasaravalli, challenged the assumption that Western aesthetics should define cinematic perfection. “I don’t want to take your aesthetic sensibility as my sensibility,” he said, quoting Espinosa. Kasaravalli said each country and each region has its own aesthetic concerns. “We should make films according to that condition; we should never imitate the West. Why should I be perfect? I should be loyal to my own milieu.”

	Asked whether parallel cinema belonged to a particular period, Kasaravalli disagreed, pointing to notable films being made across the country today. The larger problem, he said, was reaching audiences. Of streaming platforms, he said: “We all thought it is going to be a solution for all of us. But OTT [streaming] is exactly doing what the mainstream distribution network was doing earlier.”
	

	In the audience Q&A, he addressed open endings and whether a filmmaker should provide answers. “A filmmaker who says that he knows answers for all the questions in life is telling a lie,” he said. “He is also as confused as you are. He only throws up options so that you can start thinking. There is nothing called closure… life is always open.”

	As the session concluded, IFFI festival director Ashutosh Gowariker described Kasaravalli’s work as “textbooks,” saying he had returned to “Ghatashraddha” while developing a new film. He also singled out the filmmaker’s close-ups. “You let your actors simply be. You make the audience think and anticipate what the character is going through,” Gowariker said.

schema.headline: Indian Auteur Girish Kasaravalli Looks Back on 50 Years of Cinema at IFFI Masterclass: ‘All My Films Talk About Othering’

title: Trump Advisor Steven Paul Hopes U.S. Tax Credit Will Be ‘Active’ in January, Tariffs Are Old News: ‘Now It’s All Hands on Deck Federal Credit’
description: Steven Paul, a special advisor to President Donald Trump who has lobbied for a U.S. federal tax credit alongside special ambassador to Hollywood Jo
body:
Steven Paul, a special advisor to President Donald Trump who has lobbied for a U.S. federal tax credit alongside special ambassador to Hollywood Jon Voight, said he hopes the incentive will be “active” in some form by January 2027.

	Speaking at the Doha Industry Days – the industry component of the Doha Film Festival – during a fireside chat moderated by Variety’s Nick Vivarelli, Paul said, “We still have a little ways to go” in terms of making the proposed tax credit a reality. “There’s a bill that’s written, and already we put together a very big coalition of almost everybody representing the entertainment business,” he added, mentioning he has the support of members from organizations such as SAG, DGA and the Writers Guild of America.
	

	“What has to happen is it has to be attached to some sort of a bill,” he continued. “This is stuff that I’ve never been involved in. This is now the politics of it all, where they all now go into sessions and negotiate with each other and all of that. So we’re hoping that it gets attached to a bill, whatever that bill will be now, in the upcoming weeks and gets voted on before the end of the year so that it would actually be active starting in January.”

	Paul serves as chairman, founder and CEO of Crystal Sky Pictures and SP Media Group. He has shepherded several box-office successes in years past, including the Baby Geniuses franchise, “Ghost Rider” and “Ghost Rider 2: Spirit of Vengeance,” starring Nicolas Cage, “Ghost in the Shell,” starring Scarlett Johansson, and the Lionsgate-distributed “Rambo: Last Blood.”
	

	The producer recalled telling Trump he was “ashamed” to be shooting his next film about the early years of Richard Nixon in England. The President, in response, said that wasn’t “right.” It was at that meeting that Paul convinced the President of the need for a federal tax credit. “Finally, he supported it, and we now have a tremendous energy behind it.”



	

					Steven Paul with Donald Trump and Jon Voight
									Courtesy of Steven Paul
	



	Asked about the intricacies of the proposed rebate, Paul said it is “between 20 and 30% government federal tax credit.” The benefit starts at a base of 20%, and then there are two uplifts: if you’re an independent production, you get an extra 5%; and if you are filming in an area “considered a disaster zone,” you get another 5%. Given the recent devastating fires, California now qualifies as a disaster zone, the producer noted.

	“That goes on top of a state tax credit,” he emphasized. “So you can go into Jersey, you can go into New York, you can go anywhere, and it goes right on top of it. That means you get both of them. You can get the 20 or 30% state tax credit and potentially up to another 20 to 30% on the federal.”

	Would a combined tax credit of up to 50% or 60% cause states to possibly reduce their local breaks? Paul “doesn’t believe” so. “I think they’ll still all want to outbid each other, so they might even increase it. I don’t think anybody’s gonna reduce their tax credits in the state. That’s my guess.”

	The producer sees the federal tax credit as essential to bring productions back to the U.S., but mentioned how, even with a combined 50%-60% credit, the country might still struggle to lure major productions away from European hubs like Hungary and Romania because of the high production costs in the U.S. “It is still probably advantageous to shoot in these other places.”

	When asked what he believes was the catalyst for the big Hollywood exodus, Paul responded with the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike. “We [ended] up not having production for a while, and then people [went] off [to] find other ways to make production.”

	“It’s almost the same way unscripted got started because there was a writers’ strike at that time period,” he said, referring to the 2007-2008 strike. “I hate these strikes. I think it’s always counterproductive. I think people should just never strike, get into a room, negotiate hard, just get something done because those strikes end up hurting everybody. You always have a failed win, and I think that was one of them.”
	

	Paul reiterated he has the support of all major Hollywood studios, including the newly-formed Skydance. “We’ve been making films with Paramount for the past eight years, and we have a relationship with David Ellison,” he said. “Even though it was competitive at one moment, we now like each other. I think it’s going to be healthy. I think there’ll be a lot more production that takes place. David is a filmmaker. He really cares about the entertainment business, and I think that’s gonna be good. I’m optimistic about that.”

	The producer said the execs “love the idea of bringing a certain amount of productions back to America.” “Our stages are empty. They all have studios. Paramount has a lot of sound stages. Everybody has sound stages, and we want them full.”

	“I’ve met with almost every head of every major studio, who are all championing it,” he continued. They themselves are getting on the phones to call people, congress-people, to help make it happen because they know how important it is for them [to hit] their bottom line.”

	Paul is “thankful” for Trump’s apparent dismissal of his previously fervent support of a 100% tariff on films produced outside of the U.S. as a way of countering foreign tax incentives. “Thankfully, I haven’t heard the word tariff. In the beginning, we were hearing tariffs all the time. That was the thing. When I came here last time, it was the tariff, but no. Now it’s all hands on deck, federal tax credit.”

schema.headline: Trump Advisor Steven Paul Hopes U.S. Tax Credit Will Be ‘Active’ in January, Tariffs Are Old News: ‘Now It’s All Hands on Deck Federal Credit’

title: Melania Trump Calls for ‘Peace’ When Asked About Children in Gaza and Israel at Amazon Series Premiere
description: Amazon Prime Video’s “Melania: The Series” offers a peek into the often-reclusive first lady’s personal life and role inside the White House, inclu
body:
Amazon Prime Video’s “Melania: The Series” offers a peek into the often-reclusive first lady’s personal life and role inside the White House, including her efforts to provide children in foster care with educational and career opportunities.

	But as the first lady seeks a more public-facing role in international peacemaking efforts, most recently taking credit for brokering a ceasefire in Ukraine, how often does she think about the children in Gaza, Israel and other parts of the world affected by conflict?
	

	When posed the question at the New York premiere of her new two-part Amazon series, the first lady told Variety: “I want peace all around the world. That’s very important to me. We should all live in harmony and peace.”

	“I hope we can,” she added, before vaguely suggesting how that peace might be achieved: “To get together.”

	The first lady’s call for peace comes at a pivotal moment in President Donald Trump’s presidency, one where he attempts to recast himself as a global peacemaker after a bruising midterm defeat. (In the wake of the “blue wave,” Vice President JD Vance identified “end[ing] the war” and “chang[ing] our relationship to Israel” as two of the “top four causes” he and his most trusted pollsters believe could win back Republican voters who flipped their votes.)

	Efforts “to get together” were underway just hours before the Prime Video series premiere, as Presidents Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin convened for a historic trilateral summit in China. The meeting culminated in a joint declaration emphasizing peace, commitments to the United Nations and a reaffirmation that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”
	

	While Trump celebrated the meeting as a historic breakthrough (fittingly rating his trip a “12” out of 10), some foreign policy analysts argued that the summit was more spectacle than substance and raised concerns over legitimizing Putin without securing concessions on Ukraine. The joint declaration also did not directly address the ongoing conflicts in Gaza or Iran.

	The two-part docuseries is the second project released under Amazon’s $40 million licensing agreement for the Brett Ratner-directed “Melania” documentary, which debuted in January. Producer Marc Beckman oversaw the bidding war for what he calls “the biggest documentary in history.” (While the film exceeded box office expectations, its $16.6 million worldwide gross falls far short of the all-time documentary record. To put it in perspective, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “You Can See Everything” earned more in its second weekend playing in U.S. theaters alone than “Melania” did during its entire worldwide run.)

	“I went to multiple entities, from Amazon to Netflix to Hulu to Paramount, and all of them were interested in picking up the film,” Beckman said. “I can tell you point-blank, Amazon’s team was honestly the best in Hollywood. They understood how important it was to get this story out. It’s a piece of history. It’s never been told before, and we were really impressed with the leadership at Amazon. Really great people.”

	Did Jeff Bezos participate? “No, he never was involved,” Beckman claimed. “He wasn’t involved in the negotiation, and he wasn’t involved in anything else.” (Democratic lawmakers, including Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have accused Bezos’ company of “bribery in plain sight,” alleging that Amazon vastly overpaid for the rights and outbid its rivals by a wide margin to curry favor with the Trump administration. Bezos defended the purchase as “a very wise business decision.”

	“Melania: The Series” is now streaming on Prime Video.

schema.headline: Melania Trump Calls for ‘Peace’ When Asked About Children in Gaza and Israel at Amazon Series Premiere

title: Marion Cotillard Says ‘I’m Not Here to Judge Movies’ as Marrakech Jury President and ‘Doesn’t Want Any Information’ Before Watching: ‘Like a Virgin’
description: Marion Cotillard, who serves as the jury president at this year’s Marrakech Film Festival, says she prefers watching films with “as little informat
body:
Marion Cotillard, who serves as the jury president at this year’s Marrakech Film Festival, says she prefers watching films with “as little information as possible.”

	“I don’t know anything about the movies we’re gonna see, I haven’t seen a single image,” the Oscar-winning French actress said at the festival’s jury press conference on Saturday morning. “That’s how I love to see movies, I don’t want to have any information.”


	“I want to be like a virgin,” she quipped.
	

	Ironically, she said she doesn’t think her role on the jury is to “judge movies.” “I consider myself as part of an audience: I’m here to be touched, to be taken by stories.”

	Cotillard was also asked about “Inception,” in which she starred alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. Does she understand Christopher Nolan’s famously complex film? “I don’t know…I thought I had,” she said to laughter. “Maybe I have. And maybe I haven’t.”

	The nine-member jury includes “Sex Education” and “Barbie” star Emma Mackey; “Phantom Thread” standout Vicky Krieps; Danish actor Claes Bang, who featured in Ruben Östlund’s Palme d’Or winner “The Square”; French actor-turned-director director Gilles Lellouche, known for “Beating Hearts”; “The Voice of Hind Rajab” helmer Kaouther Ben Hania; “All of Us Strangers” filmmaker Andrew Haigh; Franco-Senegalese helmer Ramata-Toulaye Sy; and Moroccan director-producer Saïd Hamich Benlarbi.

	The jury will award the festival’s Étoile d’Or to one of the 14 films in competition, which consists of first and second features.

	Cotillard said her only expectation she has in helping to select this year’s competition winner is “to be shaken, to be moved.”  
	

	“When I can watch a movie and I can laugh and smile and be questioned at the same time,” she continued. “When there’s a story that on the paper I wouldn’t be very interested [in] and the filmmaker who tells the story will open a new vision for me.”

	She summed it up simply: “How do you judge art anyway?”

	Mackey agrees with Cotillard that her role on the jury is to “receive the films as a spectator. “We’re here to learn, its very pure somehow,” the “Sex Education” star said. “I don’t pretend that I know everything and I’m here to learn and to absorb these films as as a cinema lover.”

	“It’s an honor and I’m happy to spend a week watching two films a day, that’s amazing,” she added. 

	Jury members were also asked about the relatively strong female representation at Marrakech and its broader implications for gender equality in the industry. This year, women hold a majority of seats on the nine-member jury while six of the 14 films in competition were directed by women.

	Krieps pointed to her role as an Irish maid in Ryan Murphy’s “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story” to illustrate the importance of female representation on screen. “I think women have had the role of oppressed and silent,” she said. “Often we had to hide, we had to disappear because otherwise we weren’t safe.”

	“I think the role I play in ‘Monster’ is someone who becomes very visible in a time when people were supposed to be invisible,” she continued, adding that her character’s wild red hair and contemporary costuming could “help people see differently in the future.”

	Sy, meanwhile, offered a more succinct response, suggesting that true progress will come when female representation is no longer a point of discussion.

	“The day when we stop counting how many women there are in juries, in jobs, as directors, then it will be normal,” the Sengalese filmmaker said to enthusiastic applause. “We have to stop asking the question and counting how many there are.”

	On Friday night, the festival opened with Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” a musical comedy starring Julianne Moore as a shy New Jersey housewife who auditions for a regional production. Though Eisenberg and Moore weren’t in attendance, the opening ceremony was still a starry affair with guests including Tilda Swinton and “Knives Out” director Rian Johnson, who is giving a talk at the festival on Sunday. 
	

	Mackey is next playing the White Witch in Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew,” and told Variety on the red carpet that she was excited to meet Swinton — who played the role in the original film trilogy — for the first time at Marrakech.

	“It’s thrilling, my absolute dream person,” she said, adding: “She’s the queen. I wouldn’t even know how to breathe around her, I don’t think.”

	The Marrakech Film Festival runs through Nov. 28.

schema.headline: Marion Cotillard Says ‘I’m Not Here to Judge Movies’ as Marrakech Jury President and ‘Doesn’t Want Any Information’ Before Watching: ‘Like a Virgin’

body:
Department of Agriculture
                          Victim of Cyberattack ...
                          Causing Concern For Country's Food Safety
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 20, 2026
                            4:09 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The U.S. Department of Agriculture was the target of a cyberattack this week ... and the breach has raised serious concerns.
      
    
              Two former USDA officials with knowledge of the matter told NBC News ... the USDA told employees on Thursday that its system for paying farmers was hit.
      
    
              The officials told the outlet that as of now, only the payment database was breached ... but the breach does raise concerns that hackers could be able to access sensitive food safety information.
      

              The government is investigating the matter, but has not figured out who was behind the cyberattack.
      
    
              The attack is the latest in tech outages and cyberattacks that have been plaguing the U.S. for over a week.
      
    
              So far, Microsoft, the FAA, banks, the NSA's classified communication system, and more have gone down at some point in the past several days.
      
    
              Trump's administration has insisted the issues are unrelated ... but many Americans are still wondering what exactly is going on.

title: 'Yes, Dear' Star Anthony Clark's Death Linked to Sepsis, Alcoholism
description:
'Yes, Dear' Star Anthony Clark
                          Death Linked to Sepsis, Flu & Alcoholism
body:
'Yes, Dear' Star Anthony Clark
                          Death Linked to Sepsis, Flu & Alcoholism
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Anthony Clark's official cause of death has been revealed ... and the "Yes, Dear" star's death certificate sheds new light on the health complications that claimed his life.
      
    
              The comedian died from septic shock on November 10 at age 63, according to a death certificate obtained by People.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The document also lists influenza A and chronic alcoholism as underlying conditions ... with acute kidney failure identified as a significant contributing factor.
      

              As TMZ previously reported ... Deadline initially attributed Clark's death to complications from pneumonia and the flu.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
              Clark's former "Yes, Dear" costar Mike O'Malley announced his passing on November 11, remembering his longtime friend as a hilarious comedian who could always get a laugh.
      
    
              O'Malley revealed the two had spoken on the phone just three weeks before Clark's death ... saying the conversation had them laughing once again.
      
    
              Clark was best known for playing Greg Warner on the CBS sitcom, which ran for six seasons from 2000 to 2006. He also starred in "Boston Common" and hosted the fourth season of "Last Comic Standing."
